entries.863bd8916a464f81f5b6c3e047283c9912d9b71e: <div sID="gen19292" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="47" osisID="Ezek.47" sID="Ezek.47"/> <div eID="gen19292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19293" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. The vision of the holy waters, their rise, extent, depth, and healing virtue, the plenty of fish in them, and an account of the trees growing on the banks of them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1-Ezek.47.12">ver. 1-12</reference>. II. An appointment of the borders of the land of Canaan, which was to be divided by lot to the tribes of Israel and the strangers that sojourned among them, <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.13-Ezek.47.23">ver. 13-23</reference>.
entries.591a3af80f32b9c3f2635232549fa16f0248b68d: <div eID="gen19293" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vision of the Holy Waters. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 574.)</title> <div sID="gen19294" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Afterward he brought me again unto the door of the house; and, behold, waters issued out from under the threshold of the house eastward: for the forefront of the house <hi type="italic">stood toward</hi> the east, and the waters came down from under from the right side of the house, at the south <hi type="italic">side</hi> of the altar. <hi type="super">2</hi> Then brought he me out of the way of the gate northward, and led me about the way without unto the utter gate by the way that looketh eastward; and, behold, there ran out waters on the right side. <hi type="super">3</hi> And when the man that had the line in his hand went forth eastward, he measured a thousand cubits, and he brought me through the waters; the waters <hi type="italic">were</hi> to the ankles. <hi type="super">4</hi> Again he measured a thousand, and brought me through the waters; the waters <hi type="italic">were</hi> to the knees. Again he measured a thousand, and brought me through; the waters <hi type="italic">were</hi> to the loins. <hi type="super">5</hi> Afterward he measured a thousand; <hi type="italic">and it was</hi> a river that I could not pass over: for the waters were risen, waters to swim in, a river that could not be passed over. <hi type="super">6</hi> And he said unto me, Son of man, hast thou seen <hi type="italic">this?</hi> Then he brought me, and caused me to return to the brink of the river. <hi type="super">7</hi> Now when I had returned, behold, at the bank of the river <hi type="italic">were</hi> very many trees on the one side and on the other. <hi type="super">8</hi> Then said he unto me, These waters issue out toward the east country, and go down into the desert, and go into the sea: <hi type="italic">which being</hi> brought forth into the sea, the waters shall be healed. <hi type="super">9</hi> And it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> every thing that liveth, which moveth, whithersoever the rivers shall come, shall live: and there shall be a very great multitude of fish, because these waters shall come thither: for they shall be healed; and every thing shall live whither the river cometh. <hi type="super">10</hi> And it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the fishers shall stand upon it from En-gedi even unto En-eglaim; they shall be a <hi type="italic">place</hi> to spread forth nets; their fish shall be according to their kinds, as the fish of the great sea, exceeding many. <hi type="super">11</hi> But the miry places thereof and the marishes thereof shall not be healed; they shall be given to salt. <hi type="super">12</hi> And by the river upon the bank thereof, on this side and on that side, shall grow all trees for meat, whose leaf shall not fade, neither shall the fruit thereof be consumed: it shall bring forth new fruit according to his months, because their waters they issued out of the sanctuary: and the fruit thereof shall be for meat, and the leaf thereof for medicine. <div eID="gen19294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19295" type="x-p"/> This part of Ezekiel's vision must so necessarily have a mystical and spiritual meaning that thence we conclude the other parts of his vision have a mystical and spiritual meaning also; for it cannot be applied to the waters brought by pipes into the temple for the washing of the sacrifices, the keeping of the temple clean, and the carrying off of those waters, for that would be to turn this pleasant river into a sink or common sewer. That prophecy, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.8">Zech. xiv. 8</reference>, may explain it, of <hi type="italic">living waters</hi> that shall <hi type="italic">go out</hi> from Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">half of them towards the former sea and half of them towards the hinder sea.</hi> And there is plainly a reference to this in St. John's vision of a <hi type="italic">pure river of water of life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.22.1">Rev. xxii. 1</reference>. That seems to represent the glory and joy which are grace perfected. This seems to represent the grace and joy which are glory begun. Most interpreters agree that these waters signify the gospel of Christ, which went forth from Jerusalem, and spread itself into the countries about, and the gifts and powers of the Holy Ghost which accompanied it, and by virtue of which it spread far and produced strange and blessed effects. Ezekiel had walked round the house again and again, and yet did not till now take notice of those waters; for God makes known his mind and will to his people, not all at once, but by degrees. Now observe, <div eID="gen19295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19296" type="x-p"/> I. The rise of these waters. He is not put to trace the streams to the fountain, but has the fountain-head first discovered to him (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Waters issued out from the threshold of the house eastward,</hi> and from <hi type="italic">under the right side of the house,</hi> that is, the south side of <hi type="italic">the alter.</hi> And again (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.2">v. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">There ran out waters on the right side,</hi> signifying that <hi type="italic">from Zion should go forth the law and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Isa. ii. 3</reference>. There it was that the Spirit was poured out upon the apostles, and endued them with the gift of tongues, that they might carry these waters to all nations. In the temple first they were to stand and <hi type="italic">preach the words of this life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.5.20">Acts v. 20</reference>. They must preach the gospel to all nations, but must <hi type="italic">begin at Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.24.47">Luke xxiv. 47</reference>. But that is not all: Christ is the temple; he is the door; from him those living waters flow, out of his pierced side. It is the water that he gives us that is <hi type="italic">the well of water which springs up,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.14">John iv. 14</reference>. And it is by believing in him that we receive from him <hi type="italic">rivers of living water;</hi> and <hi type="italic">this spoke he of the Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.38-John.7.39">John vii. 38, 39</reference>. The original of these waters was not above-ground, but they sprang up from under the threshold; for the fountain of a believer's life is a mystery; it is <hi type="italic">hid with Christ in God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.3.3">Col. iii. 3</reference>. Some observe that they came forth <hi type="italic">on the right side of the house</hi> to intimate that gospel-blessings are right-hand blessings. It is also an encouragement to those who attend at Wisdom's gates, at the posts of her doors, who are willing to lie at the threshold of God's house, as David was, that they lie at the fountainhead of comfort and grace; the very entrance into God's word gives light and life, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.130">Ps. cxix. 130</reference>. David speaks it to the praise of Zion, <hi type="italic">All my springs are in thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.87.7">Ps. lxxxvii. 7</reference>. They came <hi type="italic">from the side of the altar,</hi> for it is in and by Jesus Christ, the great altar (who <hi type="italic">sanctifies our gifts</hi> to God), that God has <hi type="italic">blessed us with spiritual blessings in holy heavenly places.</hi> From God as the fountain, in him as the channel, flows the river which <hi type="italic">makes glad the city of our God, the holy place of the tabernacles of the Most High,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.46.4">Ps. xlvi. 4</reference>. But observe how much the blessedness and joy of glorified saints in heaven exceed those of the best and happiest saints on earth; here the streams of our comfort arise <hi type="italic">from under the threshold;</hi> there they proceed <hi type="italic">from the throne</hi> the throne <hi type="italic">of God and of the Lamb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.22.1">Rev. xxii. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen19296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19297" type="x-p"/> II. The progress and increase of these waters: They <hi type="italic">went forth eastward</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.3">v. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">towards the east country</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.8">v. 8</reference>), for so they were directed. The prophet and his guide followed the stream as it ran down from the holy mountains, and when they had followed it about <hi type="italic">a thousand cubits</hi> they went over across it, to try the depth of it, and it was <hi type="italic">to the ankles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.3">v. 3</reference>. Then they walked along on the bank of the river on the other side, a thousand cubits more, and then, to try the depth of it, they waded through it the second time, and it was up to <hi type="italic">their knees,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.4">v. 4</reference>. They walked along by it a thousand cubits more, and then forded it the third time, and then it was up to their middle—<hi type="italic">the waters were to the loins.</hi> They then walked a thousand cubits further, and attempted to repass it the fourth time, but found it impracticable: <hi type="italic">The waters had risen,</hi> by the addition either of brooks that fell into it above ground or by springs under ground, so that they were <hi type="italic">waters to swim in, a river that could not be passed over,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.5">v. 5</reference>. Note, 1. The waters of the sanctuary are running waters, as those of a river, not standing waters, as those of a pond. The gospel, when it was first preached, was still spreading further. Grace in the soul is still pressing forward; it is an active principle, <hi type="italic">plus ultra—onward still,</hi> till it comes to perfection. 2. They are increasing waters. This river, as it runs constantly, so the further it goes the fuller it grows. The gospel-church was very small in its beginnings, like a little purling brook; but by degrees it came to be <hi type="italic">to the ankles, to the knees:</hi> many were added to it daily, and the <hi type="italic">grain of mustard seed</hi> grew up to be a <hi type="italic">great tree.</hi> The gifts of the Spirit increase by being exercised, and grace, where it is true, is growing, like the light of the morning, which <hi type="italic">shines more and more to the perfect day.</hi> 3. It is good for us to follow these waters, and go along with them. Observe the progress of the gospel in the world; observe the process of the work of grace in the heart; attend the motions of the blessed Spirit, and walk after them, under a divine guidance, as Ezekiel here did. 4. It is good to be often searching into the things of God, and trying the depth of them, not only to look on the surface of those waters, but to go to the bottom of them as far as we can, to be often digging, often diving, into the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, as those who covet to be intimately acquainted with those things. 5. If we search into the things of God, we shall find some things very plain and easy to be understood, as the waters that were but to the ankles, others more difficult, and which require a deeper search, as the water to the knees or the loins, and some quite beyond our reach, which we cannot penetrate into, or account for, but, despairing to find the bottom, must, as St. Paul, sit down at the brink, and adore the <hi type="italic">depth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.3">Rom. xi. 33</reference>. It has been often said that in the scripture, like these waters of the sanctuary, there are some places so shallow that a lamb may wade through them, and others so deep that an elephant may swim in them. And it is our wisdom, as the prophet here, to begin with that which is most easy, and get our hearts washed with those things before we proceed to that which is <hi type="italic">dark and hard to be understood;</hi> it is good to take our work before us. <div eID="gen19297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19298" type="x-p"/> III. The extent of this river: <hi type="italic">It issues towards the east country,</hi> but thence it either divide itself into several streams or fetches a compass, so that it <hi type="italic">goes down into the desert,</hi> and so <hi type="italic">goes into the sea,</hi> either into the <hi type="italic">dead sea,</hi> which lay <hi type="italic">south-east,</hi> or the sea of Tiberias, which lay <hi type="italic">north-east,</hi> or the great sea, which lay <hi type="italic">west,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.8">v. 8</reference>. This was accomplished when the gospel was preached with success throughout all the regions of Judea and Samaria (<reference osisRef="Acts.8.1">Acts viii. 1</reference>), and afterwards the nations about, nay, and those that lay most remote, even in the isles of the sea, were enlightened and leavened by it. The sound of it went forth <hi type="italic">to the end of the world;</hi> and the enemies of it could no more prevail to stop the progress of it than that of a mighty river. <div eID="gen19298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19299" type="x-p"/> IV. The healing virtue of this river. The waters of the sanctuary, wherever they come and have a free course, will be found a wonderful restorative. Being <hi type="italic">brought forth into the sea,</hi> the sulphureous lake of Sodom, that standing monument of divine vengeance, even those <hi type="italic">waters shall be healed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.8">v. 8</reference>), shall become sweet, and pleasant, and healthful. This intimates the wonderful and blessed change that the gospel would make, wheresoever it came in its power, as great change, in respect both of character and condition, as the turning of the dead sea into a fountain of gardens. When children of wrath became children of love, and those that were dead in trespasses and sins were made alive, then this was fulfilled. The gospel was as that salt which Elisha cast into the spring of the waters of Jericho, with which he <hi type="italic">healed them,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.20-2Kgs.2.21">2 Kings ii. 20, 21</reference>. Christ, coming into the world to be its physician, sent his gospel as the great medicine, the <hi type="italic">panpharmacon;</hi> there is in it a remedy for every malady. Nay, wherever these rivers come, they <hi type="italic">make things to live</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.9">v. 9</reference>), both plants and animals; they are the <hi type="italic">water of life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.22.1">Rev. xxii. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.22.17">17</reference>. Christ came, <hi type="italic">that we might have life</hi> and for that end he sends his gospel. <hi type="italic">Every thing shall live whither the river comes.</hi> The grace of God makes dead sinners alive and living saints lively; everything is made fruitful and flourishing by it. But its effect is according as it is received, and as the mind is prepared and disposed to receive it; for (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.11">v. 11</reference>) with respect to the marshes and <hi type="italic">miry places thereof,</hi> that are settled in the mire of their own sinfulness, and will not be healed, or settled in the moisture of their own righteousness, and think they need no healing, their doom is, <hi type="italic">They shall not be healed;</hi> the same gospel which to others is a savour of life unto life shall to them be a savour of death unto death; <hi type="italic">they shall be given to salt,</hi> to perpetual barrenness, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.23">Deut. xxix. 23</reference>. Those that will not be watered with the grace of God, and made fruitful, shall be abandoned to their own hearts' lusts, and left for ever unfruitful. <hi type="italic">He that is filthy, let him be filthy still. Never fruit grow on thee more for ever.</hi> They shall be given to <hi type="italic">salt,</hi> that is, to be monuments of divine justice, as Lot's wife that was turned into a <hi type="italic">pillar of salt,</hi> to season others. <div eID="gen19299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19300" type="x-p"/> V. The great plenty of fish that should be in this river. Every living moving thing shall be found here, shall <hi type="italic">live here</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.9">v. 9</reference>), shall come on and prosper, shall be the best of the kind, and shall increase greatly; so that there shall be a <hi type="italic">very great multitude of fish, according to their kinds, as the fish of the great sea, exceedingly many.</hi> There shall be as great plenty of the river fish, and as vast shoals of them, as there is of salt-water fish, <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.10">v. 10</reference>. There shall be so great numbers of Christians in the church, and those multiplying like fishes in the rising generations and <hi type="italic">the dew of their youth.</hi> In the creation the <hi type="italic">waters brought forth</hi> the fish <hi type="italic">abundantly</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.20-Gen.1.21">Gen. i. 20, 21</reference>), and they still live in and by the waters that produced them; so believers are <hi type="italic">begotten by the word of truth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.18">James i. 18</reference>), and <hi type="italic">born by it</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.23">1 Pet. i. 23</reference>), that river of God; by it they live, from it they have their maintenance and subsistence; in the waters of the sanctuary they are as in their element, out of them they are as fish <hi type="italic">upon dry ground;</hi> so David was when he thirsted and panted for God, for the living God. Where the fish are known to be in abundance, thither will the fishers flock, and there they will <hi type="italic">cast their nets;</hi> and therefore, to intimate the replenishing of these waters and their being made every way useful, it is here foretold that the fishers shall stand upon the banks of this river, from <hi type="italic">En-gedi,</hi> which lies on the border of the dead sea, to <hi type="italic">En-eglaim,</hi> another city, which joins to that sea, and all along shall <hi type="italic">spread their nets.</hi> The dead sea, which before was shunned as noisome and noxious, shall be frequented. Gospel-grace makes those persons and places which were unprofitable and good for nothing to become serviceable to God and man. <div eID="gen19300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19301" type="x-p"/> VI. The trees that were on the banks of this river—<hi type="italic">many trees on the one side and on the other</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.7">v. 7</reference>), which made the prospect very pleasant and agreeable to the eye; the shelter of these trees also would be a convenience to the fishery. But that is not all (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.12">v. 12</reference>); they <hi type="italic">are trees for meat,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">fruit of them shall not be consumed,</hi> for it shall produce fresh fruit <hi type="italic">every month.</hi> The <hi type="italic">leaf</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">for medicine,</hi> and it <hi type="italic">shall not fade,</hi> This part of the vision is copied out into St. John's vision very exactly (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.2">Rev. xxii. 2</reference>), where, on either side of the river, is said to grow the <hi type="italic">tree of life,</hi> which <hi type="italic">yielded her fruit every month,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the leaves were for the healing of the nations.</hi> Christians are supposed to be these trees, ministers especially, <hi type="italic">trees of righteousness, the planting of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">Isa. lxi. 3</reference>), set by <hi type="italic">the rivers of water,</hi> the waters of the sanctuary (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.3">Ps. i. 3</reference>), grafted into Christ the tree of life, and by virtue of their union with him made trees of life too, <hi type="italic">rooted</hi> in him, <reference osisRef="Col.2.7">Col. ii. 7</reference>. There is a great variety of these trees, through the diversity of gifts with which they are endued by that <hi type="italic">one Spirit who works all in all.</hi> They grow <hi type="italic">on the bank of the river,</hi> or they keep close to holy ordinances, and through them derive from Christ sap and virtue. They are <hi type="italic">fruit-trees,</hi> designed, as the fig tree and the olive, with their fruits to <hi type="italic">honour God and man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.9.9">Judg. ix. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">The fruit thereof shall be for meat,</hi> for the <hi type="italic">lips of the righteous feed many.</hi> The fruits of their righteousness are one way or other beneficial. The very leaves of these trees <hi type="italic">are for medicine,</hi> for <hi type="italic">bruises</hi> and sores, <hi type="italic">margin.</hi> Good Christians with their good discourses, which are as their leaves, as well as with their charitable actions, which are as their fruits, do good to those about them; they <hi type="italic">strengthen the weak,</hi> and bind up the broken-hearted. Their cheerfulness <hi type="italic">does good like a medicine,</hi> not only to themselves, but to others also. They shall be enabled by the grace of God to persevere in their goodness and usefulness; their <hi type="italic">leaf shall not fade,</hi> or lose its medicinal virtue, having not only life in their root, but sap in all their branches; their profession <hi type="italic">shall not wither</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.3">Ps. i. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">neither shall the fruit thereof be consumed;</hi> that is, they shall not lose the principle of their fruitfulness, but <hi type="italic">shall still bring forth fruit in old age,</hi> to <hi type="italic">show that the Lord is upright</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.92.14-Ps.92.15">Ps. xcii. 14, 15</reference>), or the reward of their fruitfulness shall abide for ever; they bring forth fruit that shall abound to their account in the great day, <hi type="italic">fruit to life eternal;</hi> that is indeed <hi type="italic">fruit which shall not be consumed.</hi> They bring <hi type="italic">new fruit according to their months,</hi> some in one month and others in another: so that still there shall be one or other found to serve the glory of God for the purpose he designs. Or each one of them shall bring forth fruit monthly, which denotes an abundant disposition to fruit-bearing (they shall never be weary of well-doing), and a very happy climate, such that there shall be a perpetual spring and summer. And the reason of this extraordinary fruitfulness is <hi type="italic">because their waters issued out of the sanctuary;</hi> it is not to be ascribed to any thing in themselves, but to the continual supplies of divine grace, with which they are <hi type="italic">watered every moment</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.3">Isa. xxvii. 3</reference>); for, whoever planted them, it was that which <hi type="italic">gave the increase.</hi>
entries.6570f5f197f2105e118c415403c664675599dff7: <div eID="gen19301" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Borders of the Land Appointed. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 574.)</title> <div sID="gen19302" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; This <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the border, whereby ye shall inherit the land according to the twelve tribes of Israel: Joseph <hi type="italic">shall have two</hi> portions. <hi type="super">14</hi> And ye shall inherit it, one as well as another: <hi type="italic">concerning</hi> the which I lifted up mine hand to give it unto your fathers: and this land shall fall unto you for inheritance. <hi type="super">15</hi> And this <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the border of the land toward the north side, from the great sea, the way of Hethlon, as men go to Zedad; <hi type="super">16</hi> Hamath, Berothah, Sibraim, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> between the border of Damascus and the border of Hamath; Hazar-hatticon, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> by the coast of Hauran. <hi type="super">17</hi> And the border from the sea shall be Hazar-enan, the border of Damascus, and the north northward, and the border of Hamath. And <hi type="italic">this is</hi> the north side. <hi type="super">18</hi> And the east side ye shall measure from Hauran, and from Damascus, and from Gilead, and from the land of Israel <hi type="italic">by</hi> Jordan, from the border unto the east sea. And <hi type="italic">this is</hi> the east side. <hi type="super">19</hi> And the south side southward, from Tamar <hi type="italic">even</hi> to the waters of strife <hi type="italic">in</hi> Kadesh, the river to the great sea. And <hi type="italic">this is</hi> the south side southward. <hi type="super">20</hi> The west side also <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the great sea from the border, till a man come over against Hamath. This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the west side. <hi type="super">21</hi> So shall ye divide this land unto you according to the tribes of Israel. <hi type="super">22</hi> And it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> ye shall divide it by lot for an inheritance unto you, and to the strangers that sojourn among you, which shall beget children among you: and they shall be unto you as born in the country among the children of Israel; they shall have inheritance with you among the tribes of Israel. <hi type="super">23</hi> And it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> in what tribe the stranger sojourneth, there shall ye give <hi type="italic">him</hi> his inheritance, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <div eID="gen19302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19303" type="x-p"/> We are now to pass from the affairs of the sanctuary to those of the state, from the city to the country. 1. The Land of Canaan is here secured to them for an inheritance (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">I lifted up my hand to give it unto your fathers,</hi> that is, promised it upon oath to them and their posterity. Though the possession had been a great while discontinued, yet God had not forgotten his oath which he swore to their fathers. Though God's providences may for a time seem to contradict his promises, yet the promise will certainly take place at last, for God will be <hi type="italic">ever mindful of his covenant. I lifted up my hand to give it,</hi> and therefore it shall without fail <hi type="italic">fall to you for an inheritance.</hi> Thus the heavenly Canaan is sure to all the seed, because it is what <hi type="italic">God, who cannot lie, has promised.</hi> 2. It is here circumscribed, and the bounds and limits of it are fixed, which they must not pass over to encroach upon their neighbours and which their neighbours shall not break through to encroach upon them. We had such a draught of the borders of Canaan when Joshua was to put the people in possession of it, <reference osisRef="Num.34.1">Num. xxxiv. 1</reference>, &c. That begins with the salt sea in the south, goes round and ends there. This begins with Hamath about Damascus in the north, and so goes round and ends there, <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.20">v. 20</reference>. Note, It is God that <hi type="italic">appoints the bounds of our habitation;</hi> and his Israel shall always have cause to say that <hi type="italic">the lines have fallen to them in pleasant places.</hi> The lake of Sodom is here called <hi type="italic">the east sea,</hi> for it, being healed by the waters of the sanctuary, it is no more to be called a <hi type="italic">salt sea,</hi> as it was in <reference osisRef="Num.3">Numbers. 3</reference>. It is here ordered to be divided among the tribes of Israel, reckoning Joseph for two tribes, to make up the number of twelve, when Levi was taken out to attend the sanctuary, and had his lot adjoining to that (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.13">v. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.21">21</reference>): <hi type="italic">You shall inherit it, one as well as another,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.14">v. 14</reference>. The tribes shall have an equal share, one as much as another. As the tribes returned out of Babylon, this seems unequal, because some tribes were much more numerous than the other, and indeed the most were of Judah and Benjamin and very few of the other ten tribes; but as the twelve tribes stand, in type and vision, for the gospel-church, the Israel of God, it was very equal, because we find in another vision an equal number of each of the twelve tribes <hi type="italic">sealed</hi> for the <hi type="italic">living God,</hi> just 12,000 of each, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.5">Rev. vii. 5</reference>, &c. And to those sealed ones these allotments did belong. It intimates likewise that all the subjects of Christ's kingdom have <hi type="italic">obtained like precious faith.</hi> Male and female, Jew and Gentile, bond and free, are all alike welcome to Christ and made partakers of him. 4. The strangers who sojourn among them, <hi type="italic">who shall beget children</hi> and be built up into families, and so help to people their country, <hi type="italic">shall have inheritance among</hi> the tribes, as if they had been native Israelites (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.22-Ezek.47.23">v. 22, 23</reference>), which was by no means allowed in Joshua's division of the land. This is an act for a general naturalization, which would teach the Jews who was their neighbour, not those only of their own nation and religion, but those, whoever they were, that they had an opportunity of showing kindness to, because from them they would be willing to receive kindness. It would likewise invite strangers to come and settle among them, and put themselves under the wings of the divine Majesty. But it certainly looks at gospel-times, when the partition-wall between Jew and Gentile was taken down, and both one in Christ, in whom <hi type="italic">there is no difference,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.10.12">Rom. x. 12</reference>. This land was a type of the heavenly Canaan, that <hi type="italic">better country</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.16">Heb. xi. 16</reference>), in which believing Gentiles shall have a blessed lot, as well as believing Jews, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.3">Isa. lvi. 3</reference>.  <chapter eID="Ezek.47"/> <div eID="gen19303" type="x-p"/>

entries.d143f7ffbade3684b81b70a0cb80361cb2113a1d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11898"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 47</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1-Ezek.47.23">Eze 47:1-23</reference>. Vision of the Temple Waters. Borders and Division of The land.</title> <div sID="gen21493" type="x-p"/> The happy fruit to the earth at large of God's dwelling with Israel in holy fellowship is that the blessing is no longer restricted to the one people and locality, but is to be diffused with comprehensive catholicity through the whole world. So the plant from the cedar of Lebanon is represented as gathering under its shelter "all fowl of every wing" (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.23">Eze 17:23</reference>). Even the desert places of the earth shall be made fruitful by the healing waters of the Gospel (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.35.1">Is 35:1</reference>).<div eID="gen21493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21494" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11898"/><hi type="bold">1. waters--</hi>So <reference osisRef="Rev.22.1">Re 22:1</reference>, represents "the water of life as proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb." His throne was set up in the temple at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.7">Eze 43:7</reference>). Thence it is to flow over the earth (<reference osisRef="Joel.3.18">Joe 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.13.1">Zec 13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.8">14:8</reference>). Messiah is the temple and the door; from His pierced side flow the living waters, ever increasing, both in the individual believer and in the heart. The fountains in the vicinity of Moriah suggested the image here. The waters flow eastward, that is, towards the Kedron, and thence towards the Jordan, and so along the Ghor into the Dead Sea. The main point in the picture is the rapid augmentation from a petty stream into a mighty river, not by the influx of side streams, but by its own self-supply from the sacred miraculous source in the temple [Henderson]. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.36.8">Psa 36:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.36.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.46.4">46:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.11.9">Is 11:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.14">Ha 2:14</reference>). Searching into the things of God, we find some easy to understand, as the water up to the ankles; others more difficult, which require a deeper search, as the waters up to the knees or loins; others beyond our reach, of which we can only adore the depth (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">Ro 11:33</reference>). The healing of the waters of the Dead Sea here answers to "there shall be no more curse" (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.3">Re 22:3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Zech.14.11">Zec 14:11</reference>). <div eID="gen21494" type="x-p"/>
entries.851e16f43731b599a1ee64c4e6f5857950c32d3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11899"/><div sID="gen21495" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11899"/><hi type="bold">7. trees--</hi>not merely one tree of life as in Paradise (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.22">Ge 3:22</reference>), but many: to supply immortal food and medicine to the people of God, who themselves also become "trees of righteousness" (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">Is 61:3</reference>) planted by the waters and (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.3">Psa 1:3</reference>) bearing fruit unto holiness. <div eID="gen21495" type="x-p"/>
entries.6fd928f4d5ffb814e76cebe8f011a3cd62e387c7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11900"/><div sID="gen21496" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11900"/><hi type="bold">8. the desert--</hi>or "plain," Hebrew, Arabah (<reference osisRef="Deut.3.17">De 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.4.49">4:49</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.3.16">Jos 3:16</reference>), which is the name still given to the valley of the Jordan and the plain south of the Dead Sea, and extending to the Elanitic gulf of the Red Sea.<div eID="gen21496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21497" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the sea--</hi>the Dead Sea. "The sea" noted as covering with its waters the guilty cities of the plain, Sodom and Gomorrah. In its bituminous waters no vegetable or animal life is said to be found. But now death is to give place to life in Judea, and throughout the world, as symbolized by the healing of these death-pervaded waters covering the doomed cities. Compare as to "the sea" in general, regarded as a symbol of the troubled powers of nature, disordered by the fall, henceforth to rage no more, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.1">Re 21:1</reference>. <div eID="gen21497" type="x-p"/>
entries.b0763b8c4177b2d023ca5d8274e70fbde5b8d2d0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11901"/><div sID="gen21498" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11901"/><hi type="bold">9. rivers--</hi>in Hebrew, "two rivers." Hence Hebrew expositors think that the waters from the temple were divided into two branches, the one emptying itself into the eastern or Dead Sea, the other into the western or Mediterranean. So <reference osisRef="Zech.14.8">Zec 14:8</reference>. However, though this probably is covertly implied in the Hebrew dual, the flowing of the waters into the Dead Sea only is expressed. Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.8">Eze 47:8</reference>, "waters ... healed," which can apply only to it, not to the Mediterranean: also <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.10">Eze 47:10</reference>, "fish as the fish of the great sea"; the Dead Sea, when healed, containing fish, as the Mediterranean does. <div eID="gen21498" type="x-p"/>
entries.25dad3219989a69cb460b3cbef085f67f5171cac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11902"/><div sID="gen21499" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11902"/><hi type="bold">10. En-gedi ... En-eglaim--</hi>En-gedi (meaning "fountain of the kid"), anciently, Hazazon-Tamar, now Ain-Jidy; west of the Dead Sea; David's place of refuge from Saul. En-eglaim means "fountain of two calves," on the confines of Moab, over against En-gedi, and near where Jordan enters the Dead Sea (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.8">Is 15:8</reference>). These two limits are fixed on, to comprise between them the whole Dead Sea.<div eID="gen21499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21500" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fish ... according to their kinds--</hi>Jerome quotes an ancient theory that "there are a hundred fifty-three kinds of fishes," all of which were taken by the apostles (<reference osisRef="John.21.11">Joh 21:11</reference>), and not one remained uncaptured; signifying that both the noble and baseborn, the rich and the poor, and every class, are being drawn out of the sea of the world to salvation. Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.13.47">Mt 13:47</reference>, the gospel net; the apostles being fishermen, at first literally, afterwards spiritually (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.19">Mt 4:19</reference>). <div eID="gen21500" type="x-p"/>
entries.8240572d516cb06ae6763b1a79b3462a6f563e5c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11903"/><div sID="gen21501" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11903"/><hi type="bold">11. marshes--</hi>marshy places. The region is known to have such pits and marshes. The Arabs take the salt collected by evaporation in these pits for their own use, and that of their flocks.<div eID="gen21501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21502" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not be healed--</hi>Those not reached by the healing waters of the Gospel, through their sloth and earthly-mindedness, are given over (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.11">Re 22:11</reference>) to their own bitterness and barrenness (as "saltness" is often employed to express, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.23">De 29:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.107.34">Psa 107:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.9">Zep 2:9</reference>); an awful example to others in the punishment they suffer (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.6">2Pe 2:6</reference>). <div eID="gen21502" type="x-p"/>
entries.f06ad06a0e85899cbaa646e449223d9614ea7146: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11904"/><div sID="gen21503" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11904"/>12. Instead of the "vine of Sodom and grapes of Gomorrah" (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.32">De 32:32</reference>), nauseous and unwholesome, trees of life-giving and life-restoring virtue shall bloom similar in properties to, and exceeding in number, the tree of life in Eden (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.7">Re 2:7</reference>; 22:2, 14).<div eID="gen21503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21504" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">leaf ... not fade--</hi>expressing not only the unfailing character of the heavenly medicine of the tree of life, but also that the graces of the believer (as a tree of righteousness), which are the leaves, and his deeds, which are the fruits that flow from those graces, are immortal (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.3">Psa 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.17.8">Jr 17:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.10.42">Mt 10:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.58">1Co 15:58</reference>).<div eID="gen21504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21505" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">new fruit--</hi>literally, "firstlings," or first fruit. They are still, each month afresh, as it were, yielding their first-fruit [Fairbairn]. The first-born of a thing, in Hebrew idiom, means the chiefest. As <reference osisRef="Job.18.13">Job 18:13</reference>, "the first-born of death," that is, the most fatal death. <div eID="gen21505" type="x-p"/>
entries.5a1cbe43936a6a2f0878999a1af76a03cf0d104d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11905"/><div sID="gen21506" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11905"/>13. The redivision of the land: the boundaries. The latter are substantially the same as those given by Moses in <reference osisRef="Num.34.1-Num.34.29">Nu 34:1-29</reference>; they here begin with the north, but in Numbers they begin with the south (<reference osisRef="Num.34.3">Nu 34:3</reference>). It is only Canaan proper, exclusive of the possession of the two and a half tribes beyond Jordan, that is here divided.<div eID="gen21506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21507" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Joseph ... two portions--</hi>according to the original promise of Jacob (<reference osisRef="Gen.48.5">Ge 48:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.48.22">22</reference>). Joseph's sons were given the birthright forfeited by Reuben, the first-born (<reference osisRef="1Chr.5.1">1Ch 5:1</reference>). Therefore the former is here put first. His two sons having distinct portions make up the whole number twelve portions, as he had just before specified "twelve tribes of Israel"; for Levi had no separate inheritance, so that he is not reckoned in the twelve. <div eID="gen21507" type="x-p"/>
entries.bebbfb776295f55d5b6f0d4c4d9eff02ee3670e4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11906"/><div sID="gen21508" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11906"/><hi type="bold">15. Zedad--</hi>on the north boundary of Canaan. <div eID="gen21508" type="x-p"/>
entries.cd364b1693acd64e1b8e9f176945edb8227c8216: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11907"/><div sID="gen21509" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11907"/><hi type="bold">16. Hamath--</hi>As Israel was a separate people, so their land was a separate land. On no scene could the sacred history have been so well transacted as on it. On the east was the sandy desert. On the north and south, mountains. On the west, an inhospitable sea-shore. But it was not always to be a separate land. Between the parallel ranges of Lebanon is the long valley of El-Bekaa, leading to "the entering in of Hamath" on the Orontes, in the Syrian frontier. Roman roads, and the harbor made at Cæsarea, opened out doors through which the Gospel should go from it to all lands. So in the last days, when all shall flock to Jerusalem as the religious center of the world.<div eID="gen21509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21510" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Berothah--</hi>a city in Syria conquered by David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.8">2Sa 8:8</reference>); meaning "wells."<div eID="gen21510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21511" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hazar-hatticon--</hi>meaning "the middle village."<div eID="gen21511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21512" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hauran--</hi>a tract in Syria, south of Damascus; Auranitis. <div eID="gen21512" type="x-p"/>
entries.97949a11b4b66006a95b7fa740897a42193b2863: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11908"/><div sID="gen21513" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11908"/><hi type="bold">17. Hazar-enan--</hi>a town in the north of Canaan, meaning "village of fountains." <div eID="gen21513" type="x-p"/>
entries.af2f3a383379c8b2eeff36aae03f804bd0e25e38: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11909"/><div sID="gen21514" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11909"/><hi type="bold">18. east sea--</hi>the Dead Sea. The border is to go down straight to it by the valley of the Jordan. So <reference osisRef="Num.34.11">Nu 34:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.34.12">12</reference>. <div eID="gen21514" type="x-p"/>
entries.564db862a89cb4d02779dfecadbef5c0aac25611: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11910"/><div sID="gen21515" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11910"/><hi type="bold">19. Tamar--</hi>not Tadmor in the desert, but Tamar, the last town of Judea, by the Dead Sea. Meaning "palm tree"; so called from palm trees abounding near it. <div eID="gen21515" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d5cd262ba5226215b9456729571d6f7960d1868: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11911"/><div sID="gen21516" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11911"/><hi type="bold">22. to the strangers--</hi>It is altogether unprecedented under the old covenant, that "strangers" should have "inheritance" among the tribes. There would not be room locally within Canaan for more than the tribes. The literal sense must therefore be modified, as expressing that Gentiles are not to be excluded from settling among the covenant-people, and that spiritually their privileges are not to be less than those of Israel (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.12">Ro 10:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.3.28">Ga 3:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.6">Ep 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.11">Col 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Re 7:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.7.10">10</reference>). Still, "sojourneth," in <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.23">Eze 47:23</reference>, implies that in Canaan, the covenant people are regarded as at home, the strangers as settlers. <chapter eID="Ezek.47"/>

entries.b47684f7790ad00e6d94990e501a8dba1bf6d179: <div eID="gen32607" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen32608" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32609" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32609" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32608" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32610" type="x-p"/> The vision of the holy waters issuing out of the temple, and their virtue; an emblem of the power of God's grace under the Gospel, capable of healing all but the incorrigibly impenitent, represented by the marshy ground that cannot be healed, <reference osisRef="Eze.47.1-Eze.47.12">Eze 47:1-12</reference>. Also a description of the several divisions of the Holy Land indiscriminately shared betwixt Jews and proselytes; to denote that in after times the privileges now enjoyed by the Jews should be also extended to the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Eze.47.13-Eze.47.23">Eze 47:13-23</reference>. <div eID="gen32610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32611" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen32611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32612" type="x-p"/> Behold, waters issued out from under the threshold - Ezekiel, after having made the whole compass of the court of the people, is brought back by the north gate into the courts of the priests; and, having reached the gate of the temple, he saw waters which had their spring under the threshold of that gate, that looked towards the east; and which passing to the south of the altar of burnt-offerings on the right of the temple, ran from the west to the east, that they might fall into the brook Kidron, and thence be carried into the Dead Sea. Literally, no such waters were ever in the temple; and because there were none, Solomon had what is called the brazen sea made, which held water for the use of the temple. It is true that the water which supplied this sea might have been brought by pipes to the place: but a fountain producing abundance of water was not there, and could not be there, on the top of such a hill; and consequently these waters, as well as those spoken of in <reference osisRef="Joe.3.18">Joe 3:18</reference>, and in <reference osisRef="Zac.14.8">Zac 14:8</reference>, are to be understood spiritually or typically; and indeed the whole complexion of the place here shows, that they are thus to be understood. Taken in this view, I shall proceed to apply the whole of this vision to the effusion of light and salvation by the outpouring of the Spirit of God under the Gospel dispensation, by which the knowledge of the true God was multiplied in the earth; and have only one previous remark to make, that the farther the waters flowed from the temple, the deeper they grew. <div eID="gen32612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32613" type="x-p"/> With respect to the phraseology of this chapter, it may be said that St. John had it particularly in view while he wrote his celebrated description of the paradise of God, Revelation 22. The prophet may therefore be referring to the same thing which the apostle describes, viz., the grace of the Gospel, and its effects in the world.
entries.d575068c8ef93d035681759bf5d438b4a1515cb3: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen32613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32614" type="x-p"/> There ran out waters - מים מפכים mayim mephaccim, the waters seem to have been at first in small quantity; for the words imply that they oozed or dropped out. They were at first so small that they came guttatim, drop by drop; but they increased so, that they became a river in which one could swim.
entries.0263b9640fc3726640bc9058456ef94fb1037752: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen32614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32615" type="x-p"/> He measured a thousand cubits - the waters were to the Ankles; a thousand more, - the waters were to the Knees; a thousand more, - they became a River that could not be forded. The waters were risen, and they were waters to Swim in. <div eID="gen32615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32616" type="x-p"/> I. This may be applied to the gradual discoveries of the plan of salvation, - <div eID="gen32616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32617" type="x-p"/> 1. In the patriarchal ages. <div eID="gen32617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32618" type="x-p"/> 2. In the giving of the law. <div eID="gen32618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32619" type="x-p"/> 3. In the ministry of John the Baptist. And, <div eID="gen32619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32620" type="x-p"/> 4. In the full manifestation of Christ by the communication of the Holy Ghost. <div eID="gen32620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32621" type="x-p"/> II. This vision may be applied also to the growth of a believer in the grace and knowledge of God. There is - <div eID="gen32621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32622" type="x-p"/> 1. The seed of the kingdom. <div eID="gen32622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32623" type="x-p"/> 2. The blade from that seed. <div eID="gen32623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32624" type="x-p"/> 3. The ear out of that blade. And, <div eID="gen32624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32625" type="x-p"/> 4. The full corn in that ear. <div eID="gen32625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32626" type="x-p"/> III. It may be applied to the discoveries a penitent believer receives of the mercy of God in his salvation. He is - <div eID="gen32626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32627" type="x-p"/> 1. A little child, born of God, born from above, and begins to taste the bread of life, and live on the heavenly food. <div eID="gen32627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32628" type="x-p"/> 2. He grows up and increases in stature and strength, and becomes a young man. <div eID="gen32628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32629" type="x-p"/> 3. He becomes matured in the Divine life, and has his spiritual senses exercised so as to become a father in Christ. In other words, the grace of God appears to come drop by drop; it is given as it can be used; it is a seed of light, and multiplies itself. The penitent at first can scarcely believe the infinite goodness of his Maker; he however ventures to follow on with the conducting angel, the minister of the Gospel, in his descriptions of the plenitude of that salvation, provided in that living Temple in which alone the well-spring of life is to be found. <div eID="gen32629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32630" type="x-p"/> 4. In thus following on to know the Lord he finds a continual increase of light and life, till at last he is carried by the streams of grace to the ocean of eternal mercy; then "Plunged in the Godhead's deepest sea, And lost in his immensity." <div eID="gen32630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32631" type="x-p"/> IV. These waters may be considered as a type of the progress which Christianity shall make in the world. <div eID="gen32631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32632" type="x-p"/> 1. There were only a few poor fishermen. <div eID="gen32632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32633" type="x-p"/> 2. Afterwards many Jews. <div eID="gen32633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32634" type="x-p"/> 3. Then the Gentiles of Asia Minor and Greece. <div eID="gen32634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32635" type="x-p"/> 4. The continent and isles of Europe. And, <div eID="gen32635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32636" type="x-p"/> 5. Now spreading through Africa, Asia, and America, at present these waters are no longer a river, but an immense sea; and the Gospel fishers are daily bringing multitudes of souls to Christ.
entries.6f50af0d7c3881a6b90f3cc9a2add94793f3beca: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen32636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32637" type="x-p"/> Every thing - whithersoever the rivers shall come, shall live - Life and salvation shall continually accompany the preaching of the Gospel; the death of sin being removed, the life of righteousness shall be brought in. <div eID="gen32637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32638" type="x-p"/> There shall be a very great multitude of fish - On the above plan this must refer to genuine converts to the Christian faith; true believers, who have got life and salvation by the streams of God's grace. The apostles were fishers of men; converts were the fish caught. See below. As the waters flow into the Dead Sea, where no fish, it is said, can live, its waters must be healed, that is, made capable of preserving life; and so its nature be thus far most surprisingly altered.
entries.a4647475d5c431b122ef78c0a5ac75aa233d62b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen32638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32639" type="x-p"/> The fishers shall stand upon it - On the above plan of interpretation these must mean - <div eID="gen32639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32640" type="x-p"/> 1. The apostles of our Lord Jesus. <div eID="gen32640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32641" type="x-p"/> 2. The preachers of the everlasting Gospel. See <reference osisRef="Mat.4.19">Mat 4:19</reference>. <div eID="gen32641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32642" type="x-p"/> From En-gedi - At the southern extremity of the Dead Sea. <div eID="gen32642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32643" type="x-p"/> Unto En-eglaim - At the northern extremity of the same. <div eID="gen32643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32644" type="x-p"/> Their fish shall be according to their kinds - Every kind of fish, and the fish all excellent of their kinds. All nations, and kindreds, and people shall be called by the Gospel; it shall not be an excluding system like that of Judaism, for its Author tasted death for every man.
entries.bbb50eab3ab5bca98a2c70e9458d4121b16a908f: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen32644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32645" type="x-p"/> The miry places - "Point out," says Calmet, "the schismatics and heretics who do not live by the Spirit of Jesus Christ, but separate from his Church; and the evil Christians who dishonor that Church, of which they are corrupt members." A description applicable to the Roman Catholic Church, that is both schismatic and heretic from the Church of Jesus Christ, which is built on the foundation of the prophets and apostles, Jesus himself being the chief corner stone; for the Church of Rome, leaving this foundation, is now built on the foundation of councils and traditions, and lying miracles; the popes in their succession being its only corner stones.
entries.2efbf75047748de253e2c688ad69b1edd2bad66c: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen32645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32646" type="x-p"/> Shall grow all trees for meat, whose leaf shall not fade - A description that suits the righteous, who are still producing - <div eID="gen32646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32647" type="x-p"/> 1. The fruits of faith. <div eID="gen32647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32648" type="x-p"/> 2. The fruits of the Spirit. <div eID="gen32648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32649" type="x-p"/> 3. The fruits of love to God, obedience to his holy will, and love to all men. Benevolence, mercy, charity, kindness, etc. <div eID="gen32649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32650" type="x-p"/> The leaf thereof for medicine - See <reference osisRef="Rev.22.1-Rev.22.5">Rev 22:1-5</reference>. Even the leaves, the holy profession of the righteous, is a spiritual medicine. Righteousness is thus encouraged in the world. The profession points out the salvation, as it shows the nature and sufficiency of that salvation; for a just creed contains all the articles of the Christian faith.
entries.7588b542e9bb12a76b034804a67542f448afe567: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen32650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32651" type="x-p"/> Joseph shall have two portions - That is, In Ephraim and Manasseh, his two sons, who each had a separate inheritance.
entries.46593c132fff2fbb2da5aab803d6b1bdd91b07a0: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen32651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32652" type="x-p"/> The way of Hethlon, as men go to Zedad - Probably Hethlon is the same as Cuthlon, a city of Syria, between Antioch and Laodicea, according to Antoninus. Some of these places are not known; but see the same kind of division, <reference osisRef="Num.34.7-Num.34.12">Num 34:7-12</reference>.
entries.bf0fbacb974b7950a3645301bc00302fe5aca7d0: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen32652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32653" type="x-p"/> Hamath - Emesa or Amesa, in Syria. - Calmet. <div eID="gen32653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32654" type="x-p"/> Berothah - Berytus, now Baruth or Beeroth, which David took from Hadarezer, king of Syria, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.8">2Sam 8:8</reference>; but these things are very uncertain. <div eID="gen32654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32655" type="x-p"/> Sibraim - Sabarim or Sepharvaim, according to the Syriac, between Hamath and Damascus. <div eID="gen32655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32656" type="x-p"/> Hazar-hatticon - The middle Hazar; or middle village, as the margin. <div eID="gen32656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32657" type="x-p"/> Hauran - The city Aurana, and the district Auranitis, are in the north-east limit of the Holy Land.
entries.30b5136a6f419ae7e1342a0b5e602363bfc31e9a: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen32657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32658" type="x-p"/> The border from the sea - The north border eastward is ascertained <reference osisRef="Eze.47.15">Eze 47:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.47.16">Eze 47:16</reference>; here it is shown how far it extends itself northward. <div eID="gen32658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32659" type="x-p"/> Hazar-enan - The village of Enan, <reference osisRef="Num.34.9">Num 34:9</reference>, placed to the north of Caesarea Philippi. Ziphron, see <reference osisRef="Num.34.9">Num 34:9</reference>, called Zaphion by the Syriac.
entries.b89a46b9693c849a53253b75e3e2185a4651c196: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen32659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32660" type="x-p"/> The east sea - The same as the Dead Sea.
entries.f01308376cf532980ce3181e2a9b48d5417bea86: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen32660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32661" type="x-p"/> Tamar - Called Hazazon Tamar, or Engedi, <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.2">2Chr 20:2</reference>. <div eID="gen32661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32662" type="x-p"/> The river - Besor, which runs into the sea near Gaza.
entries.64b554c0d78a19933fc437f14b9823fdb8646ff6: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen32662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32663" type="x-p"/> The great sea - The Mediterranean. <div eID="gen32663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32664" type="x-p"/> From the border - The southern border, mentioned <reference osisRef="Eze.47.19">Eze 47:19</reference>.
entries.75b10a4d83fd6833dcbf67562796702584e3e0dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen32664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32665" type="x-p"/> And to the strangers that sojourn - In former divisions of the land, no place was given to strangers; but in this division, (which seems to have no other reference than to the Gospel, for literally such a division never took place), the strangers are to have an inheritance; intimating the calling of the Gentiles into the Church of Christ, to an inheritance that is incorruptible, undefiled, and that fadeth not away. Glory be to God for his unspeakable gift! Amen. Amen.  <chapter eID="Ezek.47"/> <div eID="gen32665" type="x-p"/>

entries.ec250d88fcf1c2e5e07dfa6c20dd408f411a90de: <div eID="gen15355" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Blessing of the Land of Canaan, and Distribution of It Among the Tribes of Israel - Ezekiel 47-48</title> <div sID="gen15356" type="x-p"/> After Ezekiel had seen the entrance of the glory of the Lord into the new temple, which was measured before his eyes, and had received the new <hi type="italic">thorah</hi> to be announced to the people concerning the service which Israel was to render to its God in the new sanctuary, a stream of living water was shown to him, proceeding from the threshold of the temple, flowing to the Arabah, and emptying itself into the Dead Sea, to fertilize the barren soil, and fill the salt water of the Dead Sea with vital power (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1-Ezek.47.12">Eze 47:1-12</reference>); and finally, the command of the Lord is communicated to him concerning the boundaries of the holy land, its distribution among the twelve tribes of Israel, and the building of the holy city (Ezekiel 47:13-48:35). <div eID="gen15356" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The River of Water of Life</title> <div sID="gen15357" type="x-p"/> When Jehovah shall have judged all the heathen in the valley of Jehoshaphat, and shall dwell as King of His people upon Zion His holy mountain, then will the mountains trickle with new wine, and the hills run with milk, and all the brooks of Judah flow with water; and a spring will proceed from the house of Jehovah, and water the Acacia valley. With these figures Joel (Joel 4:18) has already described the river of salvation, which the Lord would cause to flow to His congregation in the time when the kingdom of God shall be perfected. This picture of the Messianic salvation shapes itself in the case of our prophet into the magnificent vision contained in the section before us.<note placement="foot">Compare W. Neumann, <hi type="italic">Die Wasser des Lebens</hi>. An exegetical study on <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1">Eze 47:1</reference>-12. Berlin, 1848.</note> <div eID="gen15357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15358" type="x-p"/> Eze 47:1. <hi type="italic">And he led me back to the door of the house, and, behold, water flowed out from under the threshold of the house toward the east, for the front side of the house was toward the east; and the water flowed down from below, from the right shoulder of the house on the south of the altar.</hi> Eze 47:2. <hi type="italic">And he led me out by the way of the north gate, and caused me to go round about on the outside, to the outer gate of the way to the (gate), looking toward the east; and, behold, waters rippled for the right shoulder of the gate.</hi> Eze 47:3. <hi type="italic">When the man went out toward the east, he had a measuring line in his hand, and he measured a thousand cubits, and caused me to go through the water-water to the ankles.</hi> Eze 47:4. <hi type="italic">And he measured a thousand, and caused me to go through the water-water to the knees; and he measured a thousand, and caused me to go through-water to the hips.</hi> Eze 47:5. <hi type="italic">And he measured a thousand-a river through which I could not walk, for the water was high, water to swim in, a river which could not be forded.</hi> Eze 47:6. <hi type="italic">And he said to me, Hast thou seen it, son of man? and he led me back again by the bank of the river.</hi> Eze 47:7. <hi type="italic">When I returned, behold, there stood on the bank of the river very many trees on this side and on that.</hi> Eze 47:8. <hi type="italic">And he said to me, This water flows out into the eastern circle, and runs down into the plain, and reaches the sea; into the sea is it carried out, that the waters may become wholesome.</hi> Eze 47:9. <hi type="italic">And it will come to pass, every living thing with which it swarms everywhere, whither the double river comes, will live, and there will be very many fishes; for when this water comes thither they will become wholesome, and everything will live whither the river comes.</hi> Eze 47:10. <hi type="italic">And fishermen will stand by it, from Engedi to Eneglaim they will spread out nets; after their kind will there be fishes therein, like the fishes of the great sea, very many.</hi> Eze 47:11. <hi type="italic">Its marshes and its swamps, they will not become wholesome, they will be given up to salt.</hi> Eze 47:12. <hi type="italic">And by the river will all kinds of trees of edible fruit grow on its bank, on this side and on that; their leaves will not wither, and their fruits will not fail; every moon they will bear ripe fruit, for its water flows out of its sanctuary. And their fruits will serve as food, and their leaves as medicine.</hi> <div eID="gen15358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15359" type="x-p"/> From the outer court, where Ezekiel had been shown the sacrificial kitchens for the people (Eze 46:21.), he is taken back to the front of the door of the temple house, to be shown a spring of water, flowing out from under the threshold of the temple, which has swollen in the short course of four thousand cubits from its source into a deep river in which men can swim, and which flows down to the Jordan valley, to empty itself into the Dead Sea. In <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.1">Eze 47:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.2">Eze 47:2</reference>, the origin and course of this water are described; in <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.3">Eze 47:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.5">Eze 47:5</reference>, its marvellous increase; in <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.6">Eze 47:6</reference>, the growth of trees on its banks; in <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.7-Ezek.47.12">Eze 47:7-12</reference>, its emptying itself into the Arabah and into the Dead Sea, with the life-giving power of its water. - Eze 47:1. The door of the house is the entrance into the holy place of the temple, and מפתּן הבּית the threshold of this door. קדימה, not “in the east” (Hitzig), for the following sentence explaining the reason does not require this meaning; but “toward the east” of the threshold, which lay toward the east, for the front of the temple was in the east. מתּחת is not to be connected with מכּתף, but to be taken by itself, only not in the sense of downwards (Hitzig), but from beneath, namely, down from the right shoulder of the house. ירד, to flow down, because the temple stood on higher ground than the inner court. The right shoulder is the part of the eastern wall of the holy place between the door and the pillars, the breadth of which was five cubits (<reference osisRef="Ezek.41.1">Eze 41:1</reference>). The water therefore issued from the corner formed by the southern wall of the porch and the eastern wall of the holy place (see the sketch on Plate I), and flowed past the altar of burnt-offering on the south side, and crossed the court in an easterly direction, passing under its surrounding wall. It then flowed across the outer court and under the pavement and the eastern wall into the open country, where the prophet, on the outside in front of the gate, saw it rippling forth from the right shoulder of that gate. That he might do this, he was led out through the north gate, because the east gate was shut (<reference osisRef="Ezek.44.1">Eze 44:1</reference>), and round by the outside wall to the eastern outer gate. דּרך חוּץ is more minutely defined by אל־שׁער החוּץ, and this, again, by דּרך הפּונה קדים, “by the way to the (gate) looking eastwards.” The ἁπ. λεγ. ּרך̓̀ינבל;, <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> of פּכה, related to בּכה, most probably signifies to ripple, not to trickle. מים has no article, because it is evident from the context that the water was the same as that which Ezekiel had seen in the inner court, issuing from the threshold of the temple. The right shoulder is that portion of the eastern wall which joined the south side of the gate. - <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.3">Eze 47:3</reference>-5. The miraculous increase in the depth of the water. A thousand cubits from the wall, as one walked through, it reached to the ankles; a thousand cubits further, to the knees; a thousand cubits further, to the hips; and after going another thousand cubits it was impossible to wade through, one could only swim therein. The words מי אפסים are a brief expression for “there was water which reached to the ankles.” אפס is equivalent to פּס, an ankle, not the sole of the foot. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.13">1Ch 11:13</reference>, on the other hand, we have פּס דּמּים for אפס דּמּים . The striking expression מים בּרכים for מי ברכים may possibly have been chosen because מי ברכים had the same meaning as מימי רגלים in <reference osisRef="Isa.36.12">Isa 36:12</reference> (<hi type="italic">Keri</hi>). The measuring man directed the prophet’s attention (<reference osisRef="Ezek.47.6">Eze 47:6</reference>) to this extraordinary increase in the stream of water, because the miraculous nature of the stream was exhibited therein. A natural river could not increase to such an extent within such short distances, unless, indeed, other streams emptied themselves into it on all sides, which was not he case here. He then directed him to go back again על שׂפת, along the bank, not “to the bank,” as he had never left it. The purpose for which he had been led along the bank was accomplished after he had gone four thousand cubits. From the increase in the water, as measured up to this point, he could infer what depth it would reach in its further course. He is therefore now to return along the bank to see how it is covered with trees. בּשׁוּבני cannot be explained in any other way than as an incorrect form for בּשׁוּבי, though there are no corresponding analogies to be found. <div eID="gen15359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15360" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.8-Ezek.47.12">Eze 47:8-12</reference> he gives him a still further explanation of the course of the river and the effect of its waters. The river flows out into הגּלילה הקּדמונה, the eastern circle, which is identical with גּלילות היּרדּן htiw lacitne, the circle of the Jordan (<reference osisRef="Josh.22.10-Josh.22.11">Jos 22:10-11</reference>), the region above the Dead Sea, where the Jordan valley (Ghor) widens out into a broad, deep basin. הערבה is the deep valley of the Jordan, now called the <hi type="italic">Ghor</hi> (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Deut.1.1">Deu 1:1</reference>), of which Robinson says that the greater part remains a desolate wilderness. It was so described in ancient times (see Joseph. <hi type="italic">Bell. Jud</hi>. iii. 10. 7, iv. 8. 2), and we find it so to-day (compare v. Raumer, <hi type="italic">Pal</hi>. p. 58). היּמּה is the Dead Sea, called היּם הקּדמוני in <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.18">Eze 47:18</reference>, and the sea of the Arabah in <reference osisRef="Deut.3.17">Deu 3:17</reference>; Deu 4:49. We agree with Hengstenberg in taking the words אל־היּמּה המּוּצאים as an emphatic summing up of the previous statement concerning the outflow of the water, to which the explanation concerning its effect upon the Dead Sea is attached, and supply בּאוּ from the clause immediately preceding: “the waters of the river that have been brought out (come) to the sea, and the waters of the Dead Sea are healed.” There is no need, therefore, for the emendation proposed by Hitzig, namely, אל היּם הם מוּצאים. So much, however, is beyond all doubt, that היּמּה is no other than the Dead Sea already mentioned. The supposition that it is the Mediterranean Sea (Chald., Ros., Ewald, and others) cannot be reconciled with the words, and has only been transferred to this passage from Zec 14:8. נרפּא signifies, as in 2Ki 2:22, the healing or rendering wholesome of water that is injurious or destructive to life. The character of the Dead Sea, with which the ancients were also well acquainted, and of which Tacitus writes as follows: <hi type="italic">Lacus immenso ambitu, specie maris sapore corruptior, gravitate odoris accolis pestifer, neque vento impellitur neque pisces aut suetas aquis volucres patitur</hi> (<hi type="italic">Hist</hi>. v. c. 6), - a statement confirmed by all modern travellers (cf. v. Raumer, <hi type="italic">Pal</hi>. pp. 61ff., and Robinson, <hi type="italic">Physical Geography of the Holy Land</hi>), - is regarded as a disease of the water, which is healed or turned into wholesome water in which fishes can live, by the water of the river proceeding from the sanctuary. The healing and life-giving effect of this river upon the Dead Sea is described in <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.9">Eze 47:9</reference> and Eze 47:10. Whithersoever the waters of the river come, all animated beings will come to life and flourish. <div eID="gen15360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15361" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.9">Eze 47:9</reference> the dual נחלים occasions some difficulty. It is not likely that the dual should have been used merely for the sake of its resemblance to מים, as Maurer imagines; and still less probable is it that there is any allusion to a junction of the river proceeding from the temple at some point in its course with the Kedron, which also flows into the Dead Sea (Hävernick), as the Kedron is not mentioned either before or afterwards. According to Kliefoth, the dual is intended to indicate a division which takes place in the waters of the river, that have hitherto flowed on together, as soon as they enter the sea. But this would certainly have been expressed more clearly. Hengstenberg takes the expression “double river” to mean a river with a strong current, and refers to <reference osisRef="Jer.50.21">Jer 50:21</reference> in support of this. This is probably the best explanation; for nothing is gained by altering the text into נחלם (Ewald) or נחלים (Hitzig), as נחל does not require definition by means of a suffix, nor doe the plural answer to the context.  is to be taken in connection with אשׁר ישׁרץ: “wherewith it swarms whithersoever the river comes;” though אל does not stand for על after <reference osisRef="Gen.7.21">Gen 7:21</reference>, as Hitzig supposes, but is to be explained from a species of attraction, as in Gen 20:13. יחיה is a pregnant expression, to revive, to come to life. The words are not to be understood, however, as meaning that there were living creatures in the Dead Sea before the health-giving water flowed into it; the thought is simply, that whithersoever the waters of the river come, there come into existence living creatures in the Dead Sea, so that it swarms with them. In addition to the שׁרץ, the quantity of fish is specially mentioned; and in the second hemistich the reason is assigned for the number of living creatures that come into existence by a second allusion to the health-giving power of the water of the river. The subject to וירפאוּ, viz., the waters of the Dead Sea, is to be supplied from the context. The great abundance of fish in the Dead Sea produced by the river is still further depicted in Eze 47:10. Fishermen will spread their nets along its coast from <hi type="italic">Engedi</hi> to <hi type="italic">Eneglaim</hi>; and as for their kind, there will be as many kinds of fish there as are to be found in the great or Mediterranean Sea. עין גּדי, i.e., Goat’s spring, now <hi type="italic">Ain-Jidi</hi>, a spring in the middle of the west coast of the Dead Sea, with ruins of several ancient buildings (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Josh.15.62">Jos 15:62</reference>, and v. Raumer, <hi type="italic">Pal</hi>. p. 188). עין עגלים has not yet been discovered, though, from the statement of Jerome, “<hi type="italic">Engallim</hi> is at the beginning of the Dead Sea, where the Jordan enters it,” it has been conjectured that it is to be found in <hi type="italic">Ain el-Feshkhah</hi>, a spring at the northern end of the west coast, where there are also ruins of a small square tower and other buildings to be seen (vid., Robinson’s <hi type="italic">Palestine</hi>, II pp. 491, 492), as none of the other springs on the west coast, of which there are but few, answer so well as this. למינה is pointed without <hi type="italic">Mappik</hi>, probably because the Masoretes did not regard the ה as a suffix, as the noun to which it alludes does not follow till afterwards. - <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.11">Eze 47:11</reference> introduces an exception, namely, that notwithstanding this the Dead Sea will still retain marshes or pools and swamps, which will not be made wholesome (בּצּאת for בּצּות, pools). An allusion to the natural character of the Dead Sea underlies the words. “In the rainy season, when the sea is full, its waters overspread many low tracts of marsh land, which remain after the receding of the water in the form of moist pools or basins; and as the water in these pools evaporates rapidly, the ground becomes covered with a thick crust of salt” (Robinson’s <hi type="italic">Physical Geography</hi>, p. 215). למלח נתּנוּ, they are given up to salt, i.e., destined to remain salt, because the waters of the river do not reach them. The light in which the salt is regarded here is not that of its seasoning properties, but, in the words of Hengstenberg, “as the foe to all fruitfulness, all life and prosperity, as Pliny has said (<hi type="italic">Hist. Nat</hi>. xxxi. c. 7: <hi type="italic">Omnis locus, in quo reperitur sal, sterilis est nihilque gignit</hi>”) (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.29.22">Deu 29:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.17.6">Jer 17:6</reference>; Zep 2:9; <reference osisRef="Ps.107.34">Psa 107:34</reference>). - In <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.12">Eze 47:12</reference> the effect of the water of the river upon the vegetation of the ground, already mentioned in <reference osisRef="Ezek.47.7">Eze 47:7</reference>, is still further described. On its coast grow all kinds of trees with edible fruits (עץ מאכל, as in <reference osisRef="Lev.19.23">Lev 19:23</reference>), whose leaves do not wither, and whose fruits do not fail, but ripen every month (בּכּר, or produce first-fruits, i.e., fresh fruits; and לחדשׁים distributive, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.47.13">Isa 47:13</reference>), because the waters which moisten the soil proceed from the sanctuary, i.e., “directly and immediately from the dwelling-place of Him who is the author of all vital power and fruitfulness” (Hitzig).
